title: Mapping Flood Peak Distributions From Natural Conditions to Post‐Reservoir States and Vice Versa: A Simplified Analytical Framework for Uncontrolled Reservoirs With Spillways Outlet
content:
Abstract

The presence of a reservoir along a river modifies downstream flood events by storing and releasing water volumes. By attenuating the peak flows, the structure significantly alters their corresponding probability distributions, particularly in terms of the shape of the distribution. These shape changes result primarily from the reservoir capacity to variably attenuate flood peaks associated with different return periods, where the effect can range from maximum attenuation to acting as a transparent system. Since flood observations often provide limited insight into the reservoir effect, understanding the underlying physical processes is essential for accurate estimation of peak discharge distributions. Here, we propose an analytical approach to evaluate the modification of the cumulative distribution function (CDF) of flood peaks, both from natural conditions (ante-operam) to post-reservoir conditions (post-operam) and vice versa. It can be applied both to reservoir design and to the assessment of reservoir impacts based on real discharge data. In particular, the framework incorporates key system parameters and processes, including the available reservoir volume, its area, the maximum discharge of an uncontrolled spillway and the statistical characteristics of the inflow hydrograph. Some simplifications are introduced to derive an analytical closed-form solution such as assuming a triangular hydrograph shape. The potential of the method is successfully demonstrated through an illustrative example and a real case study, where it is shown how the framework effectively captures the tail behavior of the peak discharge distribution. Specifically, the proposed solution captures well the effect of large hydrological variability on peak discharge reduction.
